reason: The sources provide over 15 consistent, cross-verified facts across seven independent sites detailing Apophis's discovery, impact scare, flyby geometry, and space missions.
story: In December 2004, astronomers calculating the path of newly discovered asteroid 99942 Apophis announced an alarming forecast: a 2.7 percent chance of slamming into Earth on Friday, April 13, 2029. It became the first object in history to reach Level 4 on the Torino impact hazard scale. Subsequent observations and archival precovery images eliminated the 2029 collision risk, though lingering concerns over potential impacts in 2036 and 2068 persisted for years. Finally, March 2021 radar observations definitively ruled out any Earth collision for at least a century. Yet the 2029 encounter remains breathtaking. Apophis, a 450-meter space rock, will sweep just 31,600 kilometers above Earth's surface—closer than geostationary satellites. Visible to billions with the naked eye, its orbit will be fundamentally warped from an Aten-class into an Apollo-class trajectory as Earth's tidal forces stretch its surface, setting the stage for rendezvous missions by NASA's OSIRIS-APEX and ESA's Ramses.
angle: In 2029, a skyscraper-sized asteroid once given a 1-in-37 chance of slamming into Earth will pass closer than our high-altitude weather and communications satellites—and will be visible to the naked eye.

claims.claim: Apophis was discovered on June 19, 2004, at the Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona.
The asteroid was discovered by Roy Tucker, David Tholen, and Fabrizio Bernardi.
Apophis is named after the ancient Egyptian serpent deity of darkness and chaos, an enemy of the sun god Ra.
In December 2004, initial orbital calculations indicated a 2.7 percent probability that Apophis would hit Earth in 2029.
The asteroid reached Level 4 on the Torino impact hazard scale, the highest rating ever recorded for any object.
The close flyby will occur on Friday, April 13, 2029.
During its 2029 flyby, Apophis will pass roughly 31,000 to 32,000 kilometers above Earth's surface.
Apophis will pass closer to Earth than satellites operating in geostationary orbit.
Apophis poses no collision threat to geostationary satellites because its orbit is inclined relative to Earth's equator.
Apophis will be visible to the naked eye as a point of light moving across the night sky during the 2029 encounter.
The 2029 close approach will be visible from Europe, Africa, and parts of Asia.
Earth's gravitational tidal forces during the 2029 flyby are expected to alter the asteroid's rotation state and potentially trigger surface movements.
The 2029 encounter will alter Apophis's orbit from an Aten-class orbit to an Apollo-class orbit.
Radar observations in March 2021 allowed astronomers to definitively rule out any Earth impact for at least 100 years.
NASA's OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft, formerly OSIRIS-REx, is scheduled to rendezvous with Apophis in 2029 shortly after the close approach.
The European Space Agency is developing the Ramses mission to accompany and observe Apophis before and during its 2029 flyby.
In 2007, The Planetary Society organized a $50,000 competition to design a spacecraft mission to shadow and tag Apophis.
The Planetary Society's mission design competition was won by SpaceWorks Engineering with a design named Foresight.
Apophis is an elongated object measuring roughly 450 meters along its longest axis.

disputed: Impact energy estimates vary across sources: S1 cites 1,200 megatons of TNT, S4 notes more than 1,000 megatons, while S7 reports an older NASA estimate of 400 megatons. The script should attribute modern assessments as 'more than 1,000 megatons of TNT'.

Naming connection to the television series Stargate SG-1: S1 notes co-discoverers were fans of the show's villain Apophis, but co-discoverer David Tholen explicitly denied naming the asteroid after the fictional character, calling the link coincidental. The script should attribute the name strictly to the Egyptian mythological deity.

Exact minimum distance of the 2029 flyby: estimates in the sources range from 29,470 km (S2) to 30,600 km (S4), 31,600 km (S1), and roughly 32,000 km (S3). The script should describe it as 'around 31,600 kilometers' or 'less than 32,000 kilometers' above Earth's surface.
